pages.summary: The polynomial with given roots, or the characteristic polynomial of a matrix.
body: A polynomial is a row of coefficients, the highest power first. `poly(r)` multiplies out `(x - r(1))*(x - r(2))*...`; for a square matrix, `poly(A)` gives `det(x*I - A)`, whose roots are the eigenvalues. `roots` goes the other way.
syntax: The polynomial whose roots are the elements of `r`.
The characteristic polynomial of the square matrix `A`.

examples.title: From roots and back
examples.code:
p = poly([1 2 3])
roots(p)'

examples.title: A matrix's characteristic polynomial

pages.summary: A polynomial of a matrix: p(1)*A^n + ... + p(n)*A + p(n+1)*I.
body: The matrix powers, not the elements' (that is `polyval`). By the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, a matrix put into its own characteristic polynomial gives zero.
syntax: The polynomial `p` of the square matrix `X`.

examples.title: A matrix satisfies its characteristic polynomial

pages.summary: Polynomial division, or undoing a convolution.
body: `[q, r] = deconv(u, v)` divides the polynomial `u` by `v`: `u = conv(v, q) + r`, with the remainder `r` of lower degree than `v`. For signals, `deconv` undoes `conv` when the second factor is known.

pages.summary: The derivative and the integral of a polynomial.
body: `polyder(p)` differentiates; with two polynomials it gives the derivative of their product, or with two outputs of their quotient `a/b` as `q/d`. `polyint(p)` integrates with constant 0, or `k`.

examples.title: Both ways
examples.code:
p = [3 2 1];
polyder(p)
polyint(p)
polyder(polyint(p))

examples.title: The area under a curve

pages.summary: Partial fractions of a ratio of polynomials, and back.
body: `b(s)/a(s)` written as `r(1)/(s - p(1)) + ... + r(n)/(s - p(n)) + k(s)`: the residues `r`, the poles `p` and the direct term `k` (a polynomial, empty when `b` is of lower degree than `a`). A repeated pole gets terms in rising powers. Given `r`, `p` and `k`, `residue` puts the fractions back together. This is how a Laplace transform is inverted by hand.
syntax: Back to a ratio of polynomials.

examples.title: (2s + 3)/(s^2 + 3s + 2) = 1/(s + 2) + 1/(s + 1)
examples.code:
[r, p, k] = residue([2 3], [1 3 2])
[b, a] = residue(r, p, k)

pages.summary: A rational transfer function applied to data: an IIR or FIR filter.
body: `y = filter(b, a, x)` computes `a(1)*y(n) = b(1)*x(n) + b(2)*x(n-1) + ... - a(2)*y(n-1) - ...` along the first dimension that is not 1 (or `dim`). With `a = 1` it is a moving weighted sum (FIR); otherwise earlier outputs feed back (IIR). `zi` and `zf` carry the filter's state, so data can be filtered in pieces.
syntax: From an initial state, with the final one.
y = filter(b, a, x, zi, dim)

examples.title: A moving average and exponential smoothing
In two pieces, as at once

pages.summary: Two-dimensional convolution and filtering, and convolution in any number of dimensions.
body: `conv2(A, B)` slides `B` over `A`, flipped, summing products: the full result is larger than `A`; `'same'` keeps `A`'s size and `'valid'` only the places where `B` fits entirely. `filter2(h, X)` does the same without flipping (a correlation), with `'same'` by default. `conv2(u, v, A)` convolves the columns with `u` and the rows with `v`. `convn` works in any number of dimensions.
syntax: Separable: the columns by `u`, then the rows by `v`.

examples.title: Sums over 2-by-2 blocks
examples.code:
A = magic(4);
conv2(A, ones(2), 'valid')

examples.title: Flipped or not
Edges of a surface by a Sobel kernel
In three dimensions

pages.summary: The discrete Fourier transform, and its inverse.
body: `Y = fft(X)` gives `Y(k) = sum of X(j)*exp(-2*pi*1i*(j-1)*(k-1)/n)` for each column (or along `dim`), by the fast Fourier transform. For a signal sampled at rate `fs`, element `k` is the frequency `(k-1)*fs/n`, and the second half mirrors the first for real data. `fft(X, n)` pads with zeros or cuts to `n` points; `ifft` inverts, and `'symmetric'` makes the result real.
syntax: The inverse of conjugate-symmetric data, real.

examples.title: The amplitude spectrum of a noisy signal
examples.intro: Two tones, 50 Hz at 1 and 120 Hz at 0.5, sampled at 1 kHz for one second.

examples.title: There and back

pages.summary: The Fourier transform in two or more dimensions, and the inverses.
body: `fft2` transforms the columns and then the rows; `fftn` every dimension. The inverses undo them. With `fftshift`, the zero frequency comes to the middle, where the spectrum of an image is usually shown.

examples.title: The spectrum of a square
Inverses, and fftn of a matrix

pages.summary: The zero frequency moved to the middle of a spectrum, and back.
body: `fftshift` swaps the halves of each dimension (or of `dim`), so a spectrum runs from the negative frequencies through zero to the positive ones; `ifftshift` undoes it, also for an odd length, where `fftshift` twice does not.

examples.title: Even and odd lengths
examples.code:
fftshift(0:5)
fftshift(0:4)
ifftshift(fftshift(0:4))

examples.title: A centred spectrum

pages.summary: Data with a trend removed: a straight line by default, a constant, or a polynomial.
body: The least-squares line (or polynomial of degree `n`) through the data is subtracted, for each column. Done before a Fourier transform or a correlation, it stops a drift from dominating.

examples.title: A drift removed

pages.summary: The numerical gradient: central differences inside, one-sided at the ends.
body: For a vector, the slope at each point; for a matrix, the slopes across (`gx`, along the second dimension) and down (`gy`, along the first), and so on in more dimensions. The spacing `h` is a number, or the coordinates of the points.

examples.title: The slope of x^2
examples.intro: Inside, central differences give 2x exactly for a quadratic; the ends are one-sided and less accurate.

examples.title: Arrows up a surface's slope

pages.summary: The discrete Laplacian, divided by 2N in N dimensions (by 4 for a vector).
body: `del2(U)` is a quarter of the sum of second differences in two dimensions: for `U` sampled from a smooth function, `4*del2(U, h)` is close to its Laplacian (and `4*del2` of a vector to its second derivative). At the edges the differences are extended linearly from inside.

pages.summary: The Fourier transform of data at any times, or at any frequencies.
body: `nufft(X, t, f)` sums `X(j)*exp(-2*pi*1i*t(j)*f(k))` for sample times `t` and frequencies `f`: data sampled unevenly, or a spectrum at chosen frequencies. With the defaults (`t = 0:n-1`, `f = (0:n-1)/n`) it equals `fft`. `nufftn` does the same in several dimensions. The sums are computed directly.

The defaults give fft
